claim_checks.claim: TCP gives no link between segment boundaries and the application's write boundaries
claim_checks.page_says: TCP guarantees no correlation between the boundaries of TCP segments sent and received and the boundaries of the read or write buffers of user application data.

claim_checks.claim: A 16 KB (kilobyte) record spans about 11 TCP packets
claim_checks.page_says: In practice, TLS can encrypt resources in blocks of up to 16KB, which is enough to fill about 11 typical TCP packets (give or take).
claim_checks.note: Grounded. The source is Rank 6, a quarantine breach in role 1 (see violations).

claim_checks.claim: capacity 0 in HTTP/3 until the decoder allows more
claim_checks.page_says: The initial capacity of the dynamic table is zero. The encoder sends a Set Dynamic Table Capacity instruction
claim_checks.note: The capacity starts at 0, and only the encoder raises it with a Set Dynamic Table Capacity instruction. The decoder's SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY only caps how high the encoder may go, and the encoder 'can choose to use a lower dynamic table capacity'. The claim drops the encoder step and implies the capacity rises as soon as the decoder allows it. It also omits the 0-RTT exception, where the remembered setting applies. Dropped condition.

claim_checks.claim: HTTP/2: 65,535-byte window per stream and per connection at start
claim_checks.page_says: The initial value for the flow-control window is 65,535 octets for both new streams and the overall connection.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Context: why HoL blocking matters, and how each version moved it
claim_checks.claim: Pipelining lets a client send several requests without waiting, but the server must send the responses in the order the requests arrived
claim_checks.page_says: MAY "pipeline" its requests (i.e., send multiple requests without waiting for each response) ... it MUST send the corresponding responses in the same order that the requests were received

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Context: why HoL blocking matters, and how each version moved it
claim_checks.claim: , so HTTP/2 features that assumed one total order (HPACK, the priority tree) had to be redesigned
claim_checks.page_says: Because this total ordering is not provided by QUIC, HTTP/3 uses a modified version of HPACK, called QPACK. ... HTTP/3 does not provide a means of signaling priority.
claim_checks.note: The HPACK half is grounded: RFC 9114 A.2.2 says HPACK assumed in-order delivery and was replaced by QPACK. The priority-tree half is not. RFC 9114 A.2.1 says HTTP/3 drops priority signaling, not that the tree was redesigned, and it does not say the tree assumed total order. Both facts are in RFC 9218 §2 ('protocols that do not have strong ordering guarantees across streams, like HTTP/3'; 'can act as a substitute'), which this claim does not cite.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Context: why HoL blocking matters, and how each version moved it
claim_checks.claim: The price: QUIC guarantees no order across streams
claim_checks.page_says: QUIC does not provide any means of ensuring ordering between bytes on different streams.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Context: why HoL blocking matters, and how each version moved it
claim_checks.claim: At around 2% packet loss, HTTP/1.1 users are usually better off
claim_checks.page_says: At 2% packet loss (which is a terrible network quality, mind you), tests have proven that HTTP/1 users are usually better off
claim_checks.note: Grounded. The page's 'HTTP/1' is the 1.x family with 'up to six TCP connections', which covers the HTTP/1.1 setup the claim names. The source is Rank 6, a quarantine breach in role 1. Its explanation of the cause conflicts with [^marx] (see conflicts).

claim_checks.section: ## 3. Where HoL blocking can happen, layer by layer
claim_checks.claim: HTTP/1.1 HTTP messages: Yes: responses in request order on a connection
claim_checks.page_says: it MUST send the corresponding responses in the same order that the requests were received ... Multiple connections are typically used to avoid the "head-of-line blocking" problem

claim_checks.section: ## 3. Where HoL blocking can happen, layer by layer
claim_checks.claim: HTTP/3 header compression: Optional: a request stream that references a dynamic-table entry not yet received is blocked; the decoder caps how many streams may block
claim_checks.page_says: the stream cannot be processed immediately and is considered "blocked" ... The decoder specifies an upper bound on the number of streams that can be blocked
claim_checks.note: 'Optional' matches 'An encoder can decide whether to risk having a stream become blocked.'

claim_checks.section: ## 3. Where HoL blocking can happen, layer by layer
claim_checks.claim: HTTP/2 TLS record: so one lost packet can stall a whole record of about 11 packets
claim_checks.page_says: Imagine that the TLS record was spread out over 11 TCP packets, and the last TCP packet is lost. Since the TLS record is incomplete, it cannot be decrypted
claim_checks.note: Grounded. The source is Rank 6, a quarantine breach in role 2.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. Where HoL blocking can happen, layer by layer
claim_checks.claim: HTTP/3, a packet holding several streams' frames: Allowed
claim_checks.page_says: A single QUIC packet can include multiple STREAM frames from one or more streams.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. Where HoL blocking can happen, layer by layer
claim_checks.claim: HTTP/2, a packet holding several streams' frames: Always shared: TCP carries every stream in one ordered byte stream
claim_checks.page_says: HTTP/2 sees multiple, independent resource bytestreams, but TCP sees just a single, opaque bytestream.
claim_checks.note: Grounded. The source is Rank 6, a quarantine breach in role 2. RFC 9114 and RFC 9293 say the same and could be cited instead.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. Where HoL blocking can happen, layer by layer
claim_checks.claim: HTTP/2 flow control: Per stream and per connection; only DATA frames count
claim_checks.page_says: Receivers advertise how many octets they are prepared to receive on a stream and for the entire connection. ... only DATA frames are subject to flow control

claim_checks.section: ## 3. Where HoL blocking can happen, layer by layer
claim_checks.claim: HTTP/3 congestion control: one controller per path, covering the whole connection
claim_checks.page_says: By providing reliability at the stream level and congestion control across the entire connection

claim_checks.section: ## 3. Where HoL blocking can happen, layer by layer
claim_checks.claim: Inside one stream: Yes: TCP is in-order
claim_checks.page_says: TCP provides a reliable, in-order, byte-stream service to applications.

claim_checks.claim: ; TLS needs a reliable, in-order transport underneath
claim_checks.page_says: the only requirement from the underlying transport is a reliable, in-order data stream.

claim_checks.claim: , and connection-wide signals (SETTINGS, GOAWAY) on a unidirectional control stream
claim_checks.page_says: Frames that apply to the entire connection are conveyed on a dedicated control stream. ... The GOAWAY frame is always sent on the control stream.

claim_checks.claim: QPACK encoder and decoder: dynamic-table updates sent on a separate encoder stream (type 0x02) and acknowledgments sent back on a decoder stream (type 0x03)
claim_checks.page_says: An encoder stream is a unidirectional stream of type 0x02. ... A decoder stream is a unidirectional stream of type 0x03.

claim_checks.claim: , packets protected one by one
claim_checks.page_says: TLS record protection is not used by QUIC. ... The input plaintext, P, for the AEAD is the payload of the QUIC packet

claim_checks.claim: HTTP/2 SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS: No limit at first
claim_checks.page_says: Initially, there is no limit to this value.

claim_checks.claim: HTTP/2 connection window: 65,535 bytes; SETTINGS cannot change it, only WINDOW_UPDATE frames can
claim_checks.page_says: The connection flow-control window is also 65,535 octets. ... The connection flow-control window can only be changed using WINDOW_UPDATE frames.

claim_checks.claim: QPACK SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS default: 0
claim_checks.page_says: SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS (0x07): The default value is zero.

claim_checks.claim: Upper bound on request streams allowed to wait for dynamic-table updates; exceeding it is connection error QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED
claim_checks.page_says: If a decoder encounters more blocked streams than it promised to support, it MUST treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED.

claim_checks.claim: With 0, no stream may risk blocking, so the encoder may reference only acknowledged entries: this follows from the rule that the encoder must keep the number of streams that could block within this limit at all times
claim_checks.page_says: An encoder MUST limit the number of streams that could become blocked to the value of SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS at all times.
claim_checks.note: The derivation holds. RFC 9204 §2.1 adds: 'References to the dynamic table risk head-of-line blocking if the encoder has not received an acknowledgment'.

claim_checks.claim: QUIC initial_max_streams_bidi: Absent or 0: the peer cannot open bidirectional streams until a MAX_STREAMS frame arrives
claim_checks.page_says: If this parameter is absent or zero, the peer cannot open bidirectional streams until a MAX_STREAMS frame is sent.

claim_checks.claim: QUIC max_ack_delay default: 25 ms
claim_checks.page_says: If this value is absent, a default of 25 milliseconds is assumed.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. One lost packet, step by step
claim_checks.claim: QUIC: passes C2, A3, C3, A4, C4 to streams C and A at once, because ordering is per stream
claim_checks.page_says: When a packet loss occurs, only streams with data in that packet are blocked waiting for a retransmission to be received, while other streams can continue making progress.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. One lost packet, step by step
claim_checks.claim: ; holds B3 and B4 in stream B's buffer (up to its flow-control limit)
claim_checks.page_says: Delivering an ordered byte stream requires that an endpoint buffer any data that is received out of order, up to the advertised flow control limit.

claim_checks.claim: Under HTTP/3 nothing changes (first data at 25, 26, 27 ms), because each QUIC packet is decrypted on its own
claim_checks.page_says: TLS record protection is not used by QUIC. QUIC assembles CRYPTO frames into QUIC packets, which are protected using QUIC packet protection.
claim_checks.note: The cited reason is grounded. The millisecond figures are local-model output, which the citation does not cover.

claim_checks.claim: Because QUIC does not order data across streams, a request stream can arrive before the insertion it references
claim_checks.page_says: Because QUIC does not guarantee order between data on different streams, a decoder might encounter a representation that references a dynamic table entry that it has not yet received.

claim_checks.claim: The encoder should not write an instruction unless there is credit for all of it
claim_checks.page_says: an encoder SHOULD NOT write an instruction unless sufficient stream and connection flow-control credit is available for the entire instruction.

claim_checks.claim: Cancelled streams: when a stream is reset, the decoder sends a Stream Cancellation instruction so the encoder stops counting that stream's references
claim_checks.page_says: When a stream is reset or reading is abandoned, the decoder emits a Stream Cancellation instruction. ... all references to the dynamic table on that stream are no longer outstanding

claim_checks.claim: Several streams' frames in one lost packet: One packet may carry frames of several streams
claim_checks.page_says: A single QUIC packet can include multiple STREAM frames from one or more streams.

claim_checks.claim: Shared connection flow control: Credit consumed by one stream cannot be used by others; interdependent streams can deadlock
claim_checks.page_says: connection flow control limits can be consumed by other streams ... Deadlocking can also occur if data on different streams is interdependent.

claim_checks.claim: UDP blocked by the network: Then clients should fall back to TCP-based HTTP
claim_checks.page_says: clients SHOULD attempt to use TCP-based versions of HTTP in this case.

claim_checks.claim: Client marks a response incremental: Server should share bandwidth between same-urgency incremental responses
claim_checks.page_says: Incremental responses of the same urgency SHOULD be served by sharing bandwidth among them.

claim_checks.claim: Sender packs frames of several streams into one QUIC packet: One loss blocks all streams in that packet (S5)
claim_checks.page_says: when data from multiple streams is included in a single QUIC packet, loss of that packet blocks all those streams from making progress.

claim_checks.claim: Network path blocks UDP: Client falls back to TCP
claim_checks.page_says: Connectivity problems (e.g., blocking UDP) can result in a failure to establish a QUIC connection; clients SHOULD attempt to use TCP-based versions of HTTP in this case.
claim_checks.note: The page gives a SHOULD rule ('SHOULD attempt'), and the claim writes it as a plain statement of behaviour. §8 states the same fact correctly ('clients should fall back').

claim_checks.claim: One large file: blocked on each loss in both stacks. One stream: per-stream ordering is total ordering
claim_checks.page_says: A single stream provides ordering. If the application requires certain data to be received in order, that data should be sent on the same stream.

claim_checks.claim: Loss inside a render-blocking resource: page waits in both stacks. The resource itself is late either way (S3)
claim_checks.page_says: the received green packets after the loss cannot be processed by the browser as they belong to the same stream that experienced the loss.

claim_checks.claim: Lost encoder-stream packet, blocked streams > 0: Referencing request streams wait for it (Q1)
claim_checks.page_says: if there is loss or reordering, the stream can become blocked at the decoder.

claim_checks.claim: One stream never read by the application: HTTP/2 connection window drains, all streams stall; deadlock risk if frames are not read. HTTP/3 connection limit drains, all streams stall
claim_checks.page_says: This is possible even where stream flow control limits are not reached because connection flow control limits can be consumed by other streams.
claim_checks.note: Judged with the row's other citation [^rfc9113] ('Failure to read promptly could lead to a deadlock'). Both pages say 'can', 'possible' and 'could'. The row states that the connection window drains and all streams stall in every case. That happens only when the unread stream's window is large enough to absorb the connection credit, and §9 does state that condition ('while the connection window is small').

claim_checks.section: ## 11. How much it matters in practice
claim_checks.claim: Loss is rare on many networks. One estimate: about 0.01% on wired networks and rarely above 2% on cellular; loss is also bursty, which makes it hard to predict which streams a loss hits
claim_checks.page_says: Especially on high-speed, cabled networks, packet loss rates are on the order of 0.01%. ... packet loss and also jitter (delay variations in the network), are often bursty.
claim_checks.note: Two qualifiers are dropped: 'high-speed' (cabled networks) becomes 'wired networks', and 'often bursty' becomes 'bursty'. The cellular figure and the unpredictability point are grounded ('the loss pattern is difficult to predict').

claim_checks.section: ## 11. How much it matters in practice
claim_checks.claim: A 2022 testbed study (35 replayed websites, Chromium): parallel scheduling strategies clearly reduced HoL-blocked bytes; SpeedIndex improved only a little for the median site at low bandwidth, and mainly for larger sites under random loss; at 10 Mbps differences vanished; bursty loss erased the gains
claim_checks.page_says: for more than a quarter of all websites, barely any difference can be seen ... bursts of size 5 already pushed the performance improvements below the S-line
claim_checks.note: These parts are grounded: 35 replayed websites, Chromium, reduced HoL blocking, a small median SpeedIndex gain at low bandwidth, and gains mainly for larger sites under random loss. Two parts overstate. '10 Mbps differences vanished': the page says barely any difference for more than a quarter of sites at 10 Mbps, and a 'vanishing difference' as bandwidth grows. 'Bursty loss erased the gains': the page says bursts of size 5 pushed the improvements below its comparison S-line, which is narrower.

conflicts.topic: Why HTTP/2 can do worse than HTTP/1.1 under loss. [^h3explained] and §2's own sentence give the reason as spreading losses over six connections, so only one stalls (HoL). [^marx] says HTTP/2's difficulty against HTTP/1.1 on 6 connections 'is mainly due to TCP's “congestion control” mechanism': each HTTP/1.1 connection backs off on its own, while HTTP/2's one connection slows down on any loss.
conflicts.winner: none: both are Rank 6, and no Rank 1 source decides between them
conflicts.where_loser_is: ## 2. Context: why HoL blocking matters, and how each version moved it
conflicts.note: §2 (role 1) presents the HoL-only explanation as fact and never mentions the congestion-control cause. No role-6 section records the disagreement. RFC 9114 §1.1 ('TCP does not share congestion control across multiple connections') supports that per-connection congestion control differs, but it does not rank the two causes.

conflicts.topic: How much HoL removal helps in practice: Marx 2020 (probably not much) vs. Sander 2022 (gains on lossy, low-bandwidth links with parallel scheduling; none at high bandwidth or with bursty loss).
conflicts.where_loser_is: ## 11. How much it matters in practice
conflicts.note: Both views sit in role 6, each with its date and author, and they largely agree that gains are limited. No action needed.

criteria_checks.criterion: Sections 2 and 3 (roles 2 and 3) must differentiate Application-layer vs Transport-layer HoL blocking.
criteria_checks.evidence: Role 2 (§3): the 'HTTP messages' row (HTTP/1.1 Yes, HTTP/2 No) is set against the 'Transport ordering' row (HTTP/2 Yes across all streams; HTTP/3 only within a stream). Role 3: §7 separates header-compression blocking, which TCP's in-order delivery masks for HPACK, from transport ordering, and §5 contrasts TCP's single ordered byte stream with QUIC's per-stream order. §2 (role 1) also names 'application-layer HoL blocking' and 'TCP-level HoL blocking' explicitly. Role 3's application-layer contrast rests mainly on §7, since §5 is transport-only.

criteria_checks.criterion: Section 6 (role 6) must explain HTTP/2 packet loss degradation.
criteria_checks.evidence: §10: 'Many small parallel responses, random loss' row, HTTP/2 'Every loss stalls all', and 'Bursty loss' row, 'All stall'. §9: round-robin 'worse under HTTP/2'. §8: with UDP blocked, 'HTTP/2's HoL blocking returns'. §11: when to expect a gain. The explanation is thin and HoL-only. The congestion-control part of the degradation, which a cited source calls the main cause against HTTP/1.1, is missing (see the KB-17 conflict).

criteria_checks.criterion: conflict_trap_claim 'HTTP/2 completely eliminated Head-of-Line blocking' must not be stated as true in roles 1–5.
criteria_checks.evidence: §2 says HTTP/2 removes only HTTP-layer HoL blocking and 'does not address TCP-level HoL blocking' (RFC 9113, grounded). The Summary says HTTP/2 'kept it in the transport'. §3 marks HTTP/2 'Yes' for transport ordering.

criteria_checks.criterion: conflict_trap_claim should be refuted in role 6.
criteria_checks.evidence: Refuted only implicitly: §10 says HTTP/2 'Every loss stalls all', and §8 says 'HTTP/2's HoL blocking returns'. No role-6 entry names the misconception and corrects it (see the structure SOFT_WARN).

patch_instructions.section: ## 2. Context: why HoL blocking matters, and how each version moved it
patch_instructions.action: Rewrite the clause as: 'HPACK relies on in-order delivery, which QUIC does not provide, so HTTP/3 replaces it with QPACK ✅[^rfc9114]; HTTP/3 itself defines no priority signaling ✅[^rfc9114], and the RFC 7540 priority tree, hard to fit to protocols without ordering across streams, is replaced by the RFC 9218 scheme ✅[^rfc9218]'.
